headline: Blue Origin reportedly raising $10B at $130B valuation, first external fundraise
summary: Jeff Bezos's space company is seeking its first external capital from Coatue, Bezos, and other investors, despite a recent rocket test setback.
details: Billionaire Jeff Bezos’ space rocket company, Blue Origin, is reportedly raising $10 billion at a $130 billion pre-money valuation. This significant funding round involves Coatue Asset Management, Jeff Bezos himself, and other large investors.

This marks Blue Origin's first external fundraise, with Coatue expected to invest around $4 billion. Bezos is said to be committing $2 billion, and the remaining capital will come from other investors.

The funding follows a major setback: Blue Origin's flagship New Glenn rocket exploded during testing in late May. The company is still investigating the cause but intends to use the rocket for launches later this year.

Blue Origin also needs to rebuild its Cape Canaveral launchpad, which is essential for the New Glenn rocket. Getting New Glenn operational is a top priority, especially as the company focuses on supporting NASA’s Artemis missions to the moon.

Beyond lunar missions, Blue Origin harbors ambitions to launch and operate data centers in space, tapping into a growing trend. Some of the new funding might also support its recently revealed satellite internet network, which aims to provide data connectivity to enterprise, government, and data center customers.

This fundraising effort comes shortly after SpaceX's blockbuster IPO last month, where the company raised over $85 billion at a $1.75 trillion valuation, highlighting a competitive landscape in the private space sector.

headline_marked: Slopfix charges $10,000/week to delete AI-generated code bloat, [[using AI agents to trim repositories by up to 65%]]
headline: Slopfix charges $10,000/week to delete AI-generated code bloat, using AI agents to trim repositories by up to 65%
summary: This unique service targets messy AI-generated codebases, promising significant line reductions while maintaining functionality. The irony? Slopfix uses AI itself to achieve these results.
details: A new service called 'Slopfix' is charging $10,000 per week to refactor AI-generated codebases. They get paid based on how much code they delete, with an example of reducing a 100,000-line project to 35,000 while preserving functionality.

Slopfix offers free repository analysis and only takes on projects where they can make a significant impact. Their process includes creating a detailed inventory of the application's functions, which doubles as a regression checklist.

Clients receive the slimmed-down codebase, the checklist, and guardrails like a CLAUDE.md instruction file, lint rules, and CI checks to prevent future bloat. A two-week warranty covers any issues from previously working components.

The company's founder, known as 'zie1ony' on Hacker News, stated they commit to a reduction target and clients pay proportionally. Slopfix engineers use coding agents to find and collapse redundancy, describing these tools as a "power source" under strict control.

Code-analytics firm GitClear reports an 81% increase in duplicated code since 2023, the highest rate ever recorded. Refactoring has plummeted, making up less than 4% of changed lines in 2026, a reversal from 21% in 2022.

AI-generated "vibe-coded" code often develops issues months into a project as agents lose context and reinvent logic. This has led to failures like a "vibe-coded OS" scoring poorly and an agent wiping a production database.

While the business model of untangling outsourced or complex code isn't new, the rapid accumulation of AI-generated code allows Slopfix to charge a premium. The service ironically uses the same class of agents that produced the bloat in the first place.
